findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £350k reserve maintained against possible non-extension of statutory override on pooled investment fund accounting beyond 2029
findings.detail: The council previously set aside £350k to mitigate the impact if the statutory override on accounting for gains and losses in pooled investment funds was not extended. Although the override may continue to April 2029, the council has decided to maintain this reserve against the risk of future extension denial.
findings.matters: Policy uncertainty on investment accounting treatment creates a contingent liability; the reserve protects against potential balance sheet volatility if the override lapses in 2029.
findings.figures: £350k reserve maintained
findings.quote: The Council had set up a reserve of £350k to mitigate the impact of the statutory override not being extended. In view of the fact that the override may not be extended past 2029 the authority has decided to maintain this reserve

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-treasury commercial property portfolio of £3.98m generating 6.45% return but concentrated in 11 properties
findings.detail: The council holds a longstanding portfolio of 11 commercial investment properties within the borough, valued at £3.983m. These are held for commercial return (not treasury management) and generated £257k income in 2025-26. The 6.45% return exceeds treasury yields but represents concentrated local real estate exposure.
findings.matters: This non-treasury investment concentration in local commercial property creates undiversified exposure to borough economic conditions and property market risk; material if any tenant defaults or property values fall.
findings.figures: £3.983m across 11 properties; £257k income returned (6.45% yield)
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council held £3.983 million of a longstanding portfolio of 11 investment properties within the borough. These investments generated £257,000 of investment income for the Council in 2025/26 after taking account of direct costs, representing a rate of return of 6.45%

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Strategic property investment fund showing unrealised loss: £2.8m market value against £3m book value
findings.detail: The CCLA Property Fund, a long-term strategic investment, is carried at £3m but had a market price of £2.8m at 31 March 2026. The fund has no defined maturity and the council notes that capital values will move up and down over months, quarters and years.
findings.matters: The £200k unrealised loss and exposure to property market volatility indicate potential for further balance sheet impacts if property valuations weaken further.
findings.figures: CCLA fund £3m book value, £2.8m market value (£200k loss)
findings.quote: The fair value for this fund is based on the market price which as at 31 March 2026 was £2.8 million

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: 82% of borrowing (£14m) matures within 12 months, creating high refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council's maturity structure shows that £14.02m of the £17.1m total borrowing is due within 12 months. This concentration of refinancing need exposes the council to significant interest rate risk, particularly given the volatile market conditions noted in the report.
findings.matters: High near-term refinancing need means the council must roll over debt annually; if rates remain elevated or rise further, refinancing costs will compound the already-significant overspend.
findings.figures: £14.02m of £17.1m borrowing matures within 12 months (82%)
findings.quote: Under 12 months 82

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing costs overran budget by £995k (68%), raising the cost of borrowing from 5.64% to 6.36% of revenue
findings.detail: The council's financing costs outturn was £2.45m against a budget of £1.455m, an overspend of £995k. The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increased from 5.64% to 6.36%. This reflects higher-than-anticipated borrowing costs in a volatile interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Material cost overrun on debt service reduces financial headroom and suggests either debt volumes were higher than planned or interest rates proved significantly more expensive than modeled.
findings.figures: Financing costs £1,455k budgeted vs £2,450k actual (£995k overspend); ratio 5.64% estimated vs 6.36% actual
findings.quote: Financing costs 1,455 2,450 995

findings.paper_title: Annual Audit Opinion 25_26_SBC
findings.headline: Statutory homelessness review timescales not met; breach of legal duty
findings.detail: Audit found statutory homelessness reviews were not consistently completed within prescribed legal timescales. Recommendations include obtaining written applicant agreement for timeframe extensions and implementing escalation procedures.
findings.matters: Breach of statutory duty exposes council to legal challenge and judicial review; demonstrates control gaps in a critical statutory function
findings.figures: None specified; applies to homelessness reviews tested during audit
findings.quote: In addition, statutory homelessness reviews were not completed within prescribed statutory timescales.

findings.paper_title: Annual Audit Opinion 25_26_SBC
findings.headline: Fire safety high-priority action on basement storage remains outstanding well beyond recommended timeframe
findings.detail: The Fire Risk Assessment from July 2025 identified inappropriate basement storage as requiring high-priority remedial action. As of the June 2026 audit report date, this action remains incomplete and well past its originally recommended completion timeframe.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-priority safety action indicates governance weakness; unresolved fire safety issues expose the council to regulatory enforcement and liability
findings.figures: None provided; timing indicated as 'well beyond recommended timeframe' from July 2025 assessment
findings.quote: A key issue relates to the Fire Risk Assessment (July 2025), where a high-priority action concerning inappropriate basement storage remains outstanding well beyond the recommended timeframe.

findings.paper_title: App II Detailed Capital Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme is 71% unspent: only £14.8m of £50.2m deployed
findings.detail: Across all capital schemes, the council has spent £14.8m (29%) of its £50.2m working budget in the year to date, with £35.7m (71%) remaining as slippage into future periods.
findings.matters: Significant underspend across the entire capital programme indicates the council is deploying capital substantially slower than planned, affecting both cash flow and capital delivery capability that a lender would assess
findings.figures: Total budget £50,233,419; actuals YTD £14,790,922; total slippage £35,660,685

findings.paper_title: App II Detailed Capital Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Housing Company capital investment of £21.1m is entirely unspent to date
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £21.1m net capital expenditure for the Local Housing Company but spent £0 to date, with the entire amount projected as slippage. This represents the second-largest capital commitment in the programme.
findings.matters: Material unspent capital commitments affect future cash flow forecasting and signal that major housing investment plans are not yet being deployed
findings.figures: Budget £21,062,660; spent £0; slippage £21,062,660

findings.paper_title: App II Detailed Capital Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Levelling up - Sheerness Revival shows £5.4m slippage against £15.6m budget
findings.detail: The major regeneration scheme has spent £10.2m of its £15.6m budget to date, with £5.4m (35%) projected to slip into future years. This is the largest single project in the capital programme by budget value.
findings.matters: Delays on major regeneration schemes indicate project delivery risk and affect the council's ability to deploy capital as planned; a lender needs to understand whether slippage is temporary or reflects deeper delivery issues

findings.paper_title: App III Estimated Use of Reserves
findings.headline: Business Rates Volatility Reserve drawn down by £2.5m in single year (2026/27), largest one-year drawdown in forecast
findings.detail: The Business Rates Volatility Reserve, the largest earmarked reserve at £4.9m, is planned to be drawn by £2.5m in a single year (2026/27). This is the single largest annual deduction from any reserve across the entire forecast period, indicating a material planned use of this volatility buffer.
findings.matters: Drawing a volatility reserve by over 50% in one year suggests either a specific large planned use (capital project, one-off expenditure) or confidence that business rates volatility is manageable without it; either way, it reduces the council's buffer against business rates fluctuations
findings.figures: Business Rates Volatility Reserve (4,947,123) drawn by 2,500,000 to (2,447,123)

findings.paper_title: App III Estimated Use of Reserves
findings.headline: Eight earmarked reserves planned to be fully depleted to zero by 2028/29
findings.detail: Multiple named reserves are scheduled to reach zero balance: Local Plan (zero by 2027/28), Council Tax/Housing Benefits, Waste & Street Cleansing, Kent Pool Economic Development Business Rates, Visitor Economy Strategy, Housing & Commercial Growth Business Rates Fund, Civil Parking Enforcement, and Collection Fund & grants in advance. Once depleted, these dedicated reserves cease to exist as buffers.
findings.matters: Zero balances on earmarked reserves means the council loses purpose-specific funding sources and contingency capacity in those functional areas
findings.figures: Local Plan Reserve depleted 2027/28; Waste & Street Cleansing Reserve (2,369,283) drawn to zero; Kent Pool Economic Development (3,089,770) drawn to zero; Housing & Commercial Growth Business Rates Fund (755,584) depleted by 2026/27

findings.paper_title: App III Estimated Use of Reserves
findings.headline: Total reserves planned to fall by 71% over four years, from £22.2m to £6.5m
findings.detail: The council's combined reserves (general fund and earmarked) are planned to decline consistently: from £22.2m (2025/26) to £18.2m (2026/27) to £12.8m (2027/28) to £6.5m (2028/29). This represents a reduction of over £15m in reserve holdings across the forecast period.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion of this magnitude is material to lenders assessing the council's financial flexibility and resilience; once depleted, reserves cannot absorb unexpected pressures or fund emergency expenditure

findings.paper_title: Financial Management Report - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Cloud systems migration incurred unbudgeted costs in 2025/26 for Confirm, Academy, TechOne, and IKEN.
findings.detail: Major systems moved to the cloud during 2025/26 with unbudgeted cloud costs. Confirm, Academy, TechOne and IKEN all incurred costs not anticipated in the 2025/26 budget. (TechOne had a budget but not until 2026/27; the others were unbudgeted.) These cost increases have been added to the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: This indicates that IT capital and revenue planning did not account for a major systems transition, resulting in unbudgeted spend. It suggests visibility gaps in the council's IT transformation roadmap.
findings.figures: Unbudgeted cloud costs for Confirm, Academy, TechOne, IKEN in 2025/26
findings.quote: The overspend is due to major systems moving to the cloud. Systems with unbudgeted cloud costs in 2025/26 are Confirm, Academy, TechOne, and IKEN.

findings.paper_title: Financial Management Report - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Local Housing Company (Rainbow Homes) capital project recorded £20.094m slippage with zero spend in 2025/26.
findings.detail: No capital expenditure occurred on the Local Housing Company in 2025/26, though work has commenced in 2026/27. This accounts for the majority of the £21.054m total capital slippage. Alongside this, Levelling Up funding of £5.476m also slipped due to project delays beyond the council's control.
findings.matters: A £20m capital slippage on a major housing investment scheme signals delivery risk and questions project planning and execution. For a lender assessing the council's capital programme capability, this is a material indicator of implementation risk.
findings.figures: £20.094m Local Housing Company slippage; £0 spend in 2025/26; £5.476m Levelling Up slippage
findings.quote: Major slippage is made up of the Local Housing Company (Rainbow Homes) £20.094m which will be slipped into a future year and reprofiled

findings.paper_title: Financial Management Report - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Grounds maintenance savings target of £175k delivered only £75k due to legislative changes affecting contract negotiations.
findings.detail: A £175k savings target was set against grounds maintenance, but changes in national legislation at the time of negotiation prevented the full target being achieved. Only £75k was secured, leaving the service £158k overspent. The council has added £100k growth to the 2026/27 budget to reflect actual contract costs.
findings.matters: A material savings plan failed to deliver due to external factors constraining the council's control. This indicates that savings targets may be optimistic or vulnerable to legislative/external changes.
findings.figures: £175k target; £75k achieved; £158k outturn overspend
findings.quote: The main overspend is £158,000 on grounds maintenance, which has resulted from a savings target of £175,000 that was set but not achieved due to changes in national legislation at the time of negotiation.

findings.paper_title: Financial Management Report - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Planning income fell £349k short of budget; agency costs continue due to persistent vacancies.
findings.detail: Planning application income was volatile and underperformed throughout the year (weak in September, November, and through Q4). The service remains dependent on agency staff to fill permanent vacancies from the 2024 restructure, with senior posts particularly difficult to recruit to. Together, income and agency costs drove a £570k overspend (£653k in planning activity alone).
findings.matters: Planning income is acknowledged as 'incredibly difficult to predict', yet it is material to the council's budget. Combined with ongoing recruitment challenges, this represents a structural budget weakness. A lender would view repeated planning income shortfalls as a reliability risk.
findings.figures: £349k planning income shortfall; £570k planning overspend; £653k planning activity overspend
findings.quote: The overspend relates to agency costs and reduced planning income. As demonstrated planning income is incredibly difficult to predict.

findings.paper_title: Financial Management Report - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation overspent by £698k, worsening from a £550k Q2 forecast.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs deteriorated through the year, from a Q2 forecast of £550k overspend to a final outturn of £698k. Quarter 4 saw increased placement costs and numbers of homeless placements, partly driven by evictions ahead of the Renters Rights Act. Additional grants of £374k partially offset this, and bad debts of £43k also contributed.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory duty with volatile, demand-driven costs. The fact the overspend worsened mid-year signals that forecasting confidence is poor, and the council may face sustained pressure from legislative changes.
findings.figures: £698k outturn overspend; £550k Q2 forecast; forecast-to-outturn deterioration of £148k
findings.quote: The cost of temporary accommodation was forecast to be significantly above budget at quarter 2, with a predicted overspend of £550k and the outturn position has seen a significant increase to £698k. Quarter 4 saw an increase in both placement costs and the numbers of homeless placements.

findings.paper_title: App III - App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Time-limited grant funding of £13.5m in 2025/26 reduces to £2.0m in 2026/27, forcing substitution with borrowing
findings.detail: Major grant schemes (Levelling Up £9,196k, Rural England Prosperity £462k, UKSPF £13k, Pride in Place £1,500k impact funding) all concentrate in 2025/26 and end or reduce sharply by 2026/27. This structural reduction forces capital investment to shift from grant funding to debt financing.
findings.matters: The cliff in grant income reveals the council is not reducing capital ambition but shifting the financing burden from central government to local borrowing, which impacts debt projections and affordability
findings.figures: Total capital income 2025/26 £19,858k vs 2026/27 £9,176k (54% reduction); Levelling Up £9,196k then £3,339k; Pride in Place funding £1,500k then £0
findings.quote: Levelling Up Scheme Grant/reserves 9,196 (9,196) 0 3,339 (3,198) 141; Pride in Place Impact funding grant 0 0 0 1,500 (1,500) 0

findings.paper_title: App III - App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Net capital spending increases 11-fold from £1.94m (2025/26) to £22.2m (2026/27), then drops to zero
findings.detail: The programme shows dramatic year-on-year volatility. 2025/26 requires £1.94m net financing, this more than doubles to £22.2m in 2026/27 (largely the Housing Company), then falls to zero in 2027/28. This concentration of spending in a single year creates a discrete borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Lumpy capital programmes indicate either poor forecasting or time-limited strategic initiatives, both material to debt affordability and covenant risk

findings.paper_title: App III - App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Local Housing Company requires £20.1m net borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council plans to establish a Local Housing Company funded by borrowing/reserves, with £21.062m gross spend in 2026/27 and only £969k income, requiring £20.093m net borrowing. The scheme has no spend in subsequent years shown, making it a one-year capital requirement that materially increases council debt.
findings.matters: This is a major strategic debt issuance that will substantially increase the council's borrowing and needs to be understood as part of its debt strategy and capacity for additional borrowing
findings.figures: Spend £21,062k, Income £969k, Net £20,093k in 2026/27
findings.quote: Local Housing Company Borrowing/reserves 0 0 0 21,062 (969) 20,093 0 0 0

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Cost pressures are not being offset by government funding or increased council tax — the council is boxed in structurally
findings.detail: Cost pressures are rising but government funding is not increasing despite the Fair Funding Review. The council cannot relax council tax limits or statutory fees. This creates a structural budget gap where no revenue levers remain to solve the problem.
findings.matters: If costs rise but income cannot rise, the only solution is service cuts or restructuring. The council faces a structural problem where all normal levers for balancing a budget have been exhausted.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Cost pressures are not being offset by increases in government funding or by relaxing the limits on council tax setting or on statutory fees and charges.

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: The council's reserves are being depleted year on year and this is forecast to continue over the MTFP period
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget relies on a contribution from reserves to achieve balance, and this pattern is forecast to continue. The CFO warns that it is not sustainable to rely too heavily on reserves as they will be depleted if a deliverable savings plan is not put in place.
findings.matters: Ongoing reserve draw-downs indicate the council is using one-time money to solve recurring problems. Reserves are finite; continued depletion at this rate means the council will face a crisis point when they are exhausted.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: the council's reserves continue to be depleted over the period of this financial plan.

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Swale faces structured funding cuts totalling £1.5m in 2027/28 and 2028/29 as Fair Funding Review protections lapse
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review provided temporary protection against business rate losses, but this is transitional. Funding will reduce by £720k in 2027/28 and a further £780k in 2028/29, adding to the structural budget gap that must be addressed with service cuts or efficiency gains.
findings.matters: These are known, unavoidable income reductions with no identified offsetting savings. They will require either service cuts or further reserve draws at a time when reserves are already stressed.
findings.quote: funding is reduced in 2027/28 and 2028/29 by £720k and then a further £780k.

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Swale is ranked at the higher end of financial stress risk by CIPFA's 2025 Local Authority Resilience Index, due to falling reserves
findings.detail: CIPFA's 2025 resilience index shows declining reserve levels across the local government sector. Swale's position — with falling reserves relative to other councils — places it among the highest-risk councils on financial stress indicators.
findings.matters: CIPFA's index is an independent measure of financial resilience used by lenders and finance directors. A 'higher end of risk' ranking signals material financial stress that is externally validated.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: The change in reserve balances and the reduction in the level of reserve for Swale put the council at the higher end of the risk indicators for financial stress.

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Both the main audit and value-for-money audit by Grant Thornton have raised concerns about the council's unsustainable reliance on reserves
findings.detail: External auditors have formally flagged that the council needs to develop a savings delivery plan to reduce its dependence on reserves. This is a findings point from both the main audit and the VFM audit, signalling concerns about financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Formal audit findings on sustainability indicate the council's financial position is weaker than routine reporting suggests. Audit concerns provide external validation that the situation is serious.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: audit findings reported by our external auditor Grant Thornton for both the main audit and the value for money audit have highlighted the need to develop a savings delivery plan to reduce the reliance on reserves and promote sustainability.

findings.paper_title: App III - App III - Section 25 Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: The Section 151 Officer explicitly warns that without a robust savings plan, Swale may need to issue a Section 114 notice, halting council expenditure
findings.detail: The CFO states that a deliverable savings plan is needed to avoid having to issue a Section 114 notice once the MTFP moves past the Fair Funding Review protection period. Section 114 of the Local Government Finance Act allows the CFO to halt expenditure when the council cannot maintain a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is the local authority equivalent of insolvency — it signals the council cannot fund its operations. This is an acute solvency risk that lenders must account for.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Now that there is some degree of certainty over government funding a robust savings plan needs to be developed to support the drafting of the MTFP for 2028/29 to avoid future consideration of the need to issue a section 114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Full Council Feb 26
findings.headline: Affordability explicitly stated as key constraint on borrowing strategy.
findings.detail: The strategy notes that given 'significant cuts to public expenditure and in particular to local government funding', the council's borrowing strategy must 'address the key issue of affordability without compromising the longer-term stability of the debt portfolio'. This flags that the council is under financial pressure and has limited headroom for cost overruns or adverse variances.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether affordability constraints will limit the council's capacity to service debt if revenues fall, costs rise, or capital costs overrun. The council's acknowledgment that affordability is a key concern suggests limited financial resilience.
findings.figures: Financing costs as ratio of net revenue stream: 2024/25 actual 7.61%, 2025/26 estimate 10.69%, 2026/27 estimate 8.58%
findings.quote: Given the significant cuts to public expenditure and in particular to local government funding, the Council's borrowing strategy continues to address the key issue of affordability without compromising the longer-term stability of the debt portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Full Council Feb 26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure cliff of 89% between 2026/27 and 2027/28 with no explanation in strategy.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme jumps to £31.410m in 2026/27, requiring £22.234m of borrowing, but then drops to only £3.415m in 2027/28 and £4.319m in 2028/29. The strategy document does not explain whether this reflects completion of a specific multi-year scheme or anticipated funding constraints in future years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's capital plans are sustainable and predictable. A sharp, unexplained cliff in capital expenditure suggests either a one-off programme ending or emerging constraints on future capital capacity. This affects the council's long-term investment capability and revenue generation.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure and Financing: Total Expenditure — 2026/27 £31,410k; 2027/28 £3,415k; 2028/29 £4,319k. Borrowing — 2026/27 £22,234k; 2027/28 £0k; 2028/29 £114k

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Full Council Feb 26
findings.headline: Council deliberately using short-term borrowing to save costs, exposing it to interest rate and refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly chooses short-term loans over long-term fixed-rate borrowing, assuming this will be cheaper. New short-term loans are budgeted at 4.50%, compared to higher long-term rates. The council acknowledges that 'short-term and variable rate loans leave the Council exposed to the risk of short-term interest rate rises'. The strategy depends on interest rates falling and remaining low, and on the council retaining access to short-term refinancing when £12m matures.
findings.matters: This strategy creates material interest rate risk. If the Bank of England's rate forecasts prove incorrect and rates rise rather than fall, or if other councils become less willing to lend when Swale's loans mature, the cost of refinancing £12m plus borrowing £22.2m new could increase significantly.
findings.figures: New short-term loans assumed at average rate of 4.50%; existing loans at 4.25%–4.82%; Bank Rate forecast to reach 3.25% by end 2026
findings.quote: Short-term interest rates have fallen over the past year, and are expected to fall a little further, and it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead. The risks of this approach will be managed by keeping the Council's interest rate exposure within the limit set in the treasury management prudential indicators.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Strategy 2026-27 Full Council Feb 26
findings.headline: £12m of existing loans all mature in Q2-Q3 2026, requiring refinancing in same year the council borrows £22.2m for capital.
findings.detail: The council holds £12 million in short-term loans from other councils, all maturing between April and September 2026 (Spelthorne £2m at 4.80% maturing 02/04/26; Tamworth £3m at 4.82% maturing 10/04/26; Ashfield £3m at 4.80% maturing 07/05/26 and £2m at 4.28% maturing 08/07/26; Amber Valley £2m at 4.25% maturing 01/09/26). Simultaneously, the council plans to borrow £22.234m for a £31.4m capital programme, meaning total refinancing and new borrowing needs of roughly £34m in one financial year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess refinancing risk. Concentrating £34m of borrowing needs into a single year, with all existing debt maturing simultaneously, creates significant execution risk if capital markets tighten or if refinancing appetite narrows.
findings.figures: £12m existing debt maturing April-September 2026; £22.234m capital borrowing planned for 2026/27; £31.410m total capital expenditure in 2026/27 vs £21.798m in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council currently holds £12 million of loans, as part of its strategy for funding previous years' capital programmes. The Council may also borrow additional sums to pre-fund future years' requirements, providing this does not exceed the authorised limit for borrowing of £74 million.

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Rising capital borrowing costs forcing fundamental affordability review of planned schemes.
findings.detail: Interest rates have risen significantly and remain high compared to recent years. Council signals that all planned borrowing for capital schemes must be 'fundamentally reviewed' before proceeding to ensure they remain affordable and deliver anticipated benefits. This indicates concern that previously approved schemes may no longer be viable. Capital programme drops sharply from £31.4m in 2026/27 to £3.4m in 2027/28 and £4.3m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Signals council is constrained in capital investment ambitions. Suggests capital schemes may be shelved or delayed. Borrowing costs reducing affordability headroom.
findings.quote: Any business cases which include borrowing will need to be fundamentally reviewed before any borrowing takes place to ensure the schemes remain affordable

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Additional government grant reductions of £1.5m scheduled from 2027/28 onwards as transitional protection ends.
findings.detail: Revenue Support Grant reduces by £720k in 2027/28 and a further £780k in 2028/29 as the transitional support for the business rates reset is removed. This is on top of the current year-on-year deficits. Council is challenging reduction in Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and Domestic Abuse grant with MHCLG.
findings.matters: Adds further structural funding reduction beyond initial 2026/27 settlement, deepening budget gap.
findings.figures: £720k reduction 2027/28; £780k further reduction 2028/29
findings.quote: from 2027/28 the Revenue Support Grant reduces by £720,000 and again by a further £780,000 for 2028/29

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs rising despite purchase of 52 properties to mitigate impact.
findings.detail: 300 households in temporary accommodation as at end December 2025, up from 273 at end December 2024. 69 households have been in TA for over 2 years. Despite council purchasing 52 properties to control costs, landlords are raising prices significantly in response to higher interest rates. Council acknowledges mitigation strategy is 'not a panacea'.
findings.matters: Growing welfare demand creating uncontrollable cost pressure. Council mitigation (property purchase) is insufficient. Demand driven by national housing shortage and interest rate environment, not controllable locally.
findings.figures: 300 households in TA (up from 273); 69 in TA over 2 years; 52 properties purchased to date
findings.quote: the impact of higher interest rates is being seen in significant price increases from landlords

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves will be fully depleted by 2030/31 if current trajectory continues.
findings.detail: Council holds £17.2m in reserves as at April 2025, forecast to be £15.1m by April 2026 after planned use of £2.1m in 2025/26. Document explicitly warns that this reserve position is not sustainable for addressing budget gaps beyond 2030/31, meaning time-limited financial cushion only.
findings.matters: Shows council only has 4-5 years of reserve cover before forced to make structural changes. Limits borrowing capacity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £17.2m reserves April 2025; £15.1m forecast April 2026; £2.1m planned use 2025/26
findings.quote: the Council will not have sufficient reserves to help address the budget gap after 2030/31

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Permanent £7.4m loss of business rates income from government's business rates reset.
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review and Business Rates Reset removes all growth in business rates since 2013/14 localisation. This is a structural, permanent reduction in core funding that cannot be recovered. Swale's loss is specifically quantified at £7.4m. Council previously participated in Kent Business Rates Pool which has now been disbanded.
findings.matters: Represents permanent loss of income base with no offsetting gains. Reduces council's baseline funding capacity.
findings.figures: £7.4m reduction in business rates; previously retained business rate growth since 2013/14, now reset to zero
findings.quote: for Swale this is a reduction of £7.4m for business rates

findings.paper_title: App III - App I - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £459k in 2026/27 growing to £3m by 2028/29 despite £1.4m of savings.
findings.detail: Council cannot balance budget through operational efficiencies alone. Deficit exists even after identifying savings of £1.4m and increasing fees and charges. The gap widens as government transitional support for business rates reset is removed in future years, requiring either additional savings, income generation, or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Council has structural income gap that grows year-on-year, indicating unsustainable position that will eventually force service reductions or significant restructuring.
findings.figures: £459,000 deficit 2026/27; £3m deficit 2028/29 (down from £5.4m previously forecast)
findings.quote: Estimated budget gap of £459,000 for 2026/27 even with current savings and fee increases

findings.paper_title: Main Report - Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 - Full Council
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation transition costs are unfunded
findings.detail: The budget includes provision for Swale's preparation work for local government reorganisation, but explicitly makes no provision for the transitional costs needed to support creation of the new unitary council. This is a known but unbudgeted liability.
findings.matters: This represents a significant unfunded commitment in the medium term. The council is preparing for reorganisation but has not set aside resources for the actual transition, creating a future budget shock.
findings.figures: Amount not quantified in this document
findings.quote: No provision has been made for the transitional costs to support the creation of the new unitary council.

findings.paper_title: Main Report - Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 - Full Council
findings.headline: Unfunded homelessness grant cut of £81k forces increased use of reserves
findings.detail: Despite MHCLG assurances that no council would see cuts, Swale lost £81k in homelessness funding with no mitigation. This is rare: only 3 councils nationally affected (including Thanet in Kent). The council has written to MHCLG but has updated the budget to assume increased use of reserves to cover the gap.
findings.matters: The council is burning reserves to cover a funding cut outside its control. This reduces financial flexibility for real pressures and represents a loss of autonomy in reserve management.
findings.figures: £81k reduction; only 3 councils in the country affected
findings.quote: Swale has seen a reduction of £81k of homelessness funding with no further mitigation to address the loss. I have written to MHCLG asking for their position of no change in total allocations to be honoured and have been advised that this is being looked into. Further investigation by Kent Finance Officers has confirmed that there are only 3 councils in the country that have seen a cut in the homelessness grant with Thanet also affected in Kent. We will be following up with MHCLG with the aim of receiving additional funding, but the budget has been updated to assume an increase in the use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Main Report - Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 - Full Council
findings.headline: Business rate pooling change structurally reduces Revenue Support Grant, with budget gap widening sharply from 2027/28
findings.detail: A change to how business rate pool growth is shared has materially cut Swale's RSG. Government has provided a one-off Adjustment Support Grant (£1.223m) to protect 2026/27, but this expires in 2027/28. The director explicitly states the budget gap forecast for future years increases significantly as a result, with no certainty on government action.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding loss, not a one-off issue, and signals material budget stress from 2027/28 onwards when the protection expires. A lender needs to know the council faces a cliff edge in grant funding.
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant £1.223m (2026/27 only), then £0. Revenue Support Grant falls from £8.062m in 2026/27 forecast to £7.948m in 2027/28 and £7.791m in 2028/29.
findings.quote: the change to the assumption on how Business Rate Pools share business rate growth has significantly reduced the Revenue Support Grant allocation for Swale and as the Adjustment Support Grant is a one off protection arrangement for 2026/27 the budget gap forecast for future years increases significantly

findings.paper_title: App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Leisure Centre Improvements will require £2m borrowing in 2026/27, stepping up from £287k in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Leisure capital spending accelerates from £287k in 2025/26 to £2m in 2026/27, both funded by borrowing. No further spending is planned in 2027/28, suggesting a discrete, time-limited capital project.
findings.matters: Major capital investment in discretionary services (leisure) signals the council's assessment of borrowing headroom and priorities; discretionary assets are typically vulnerable to deferral if financial pressures emerge, so large commitments reflect current financial confidence.

findings.paper_title: App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Council is borrowing £1.37m to purchase temporary accommodation in 2025/26, indicating housing demand pressure.
findings.detail: A dedicated capital scheme for temporary accommodation purchases via borrowing suggests demand for temporary housing exceeds existing council stock. The scheme does not continue in later years, indicating an immediate, one-off capital response.
findings.matters: Growth in temporary accommodation is a leading indicator of housing stress in the area and typically creates ongoing revenue pressure (temporary housing costs more per unit than permanent solutions), affecting financial sustainability and budget forecasts.
findings.figures: £1,370k borrowing in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: App VI - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Local Housing Company capital spending will require £20.1m net borrowing in 2026/27, concentrated in a single year.
findings.detail: The scheme shows zero activity in 2025/26, then steps up to £21.062m spend in 2026/27 with only £969k income recovery, leaving net borrowing of £20.093m. This drops to zero in 2027/28, suggesting a time-limited capital commitment, likely for housing stock acquisition or development.
findings.matters: A £20m borrowing requirement in a single year materially affects debt profiles and borrowing capacity. This scheme alone represents 64% of the council's total net capital spending in 2026/27 (£31.4m), signalling significant housing investment and debt take-on.
findings.figures: £21,062k spend, £969k income, £20,093k net borrowing in 2026/27; represents 64% of total 2026/27 capital spending of £31,410k

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation expansion requires £1.37m borrowing in 2025/26
findings.detail: Purchase of Temporary Accommodation is funded entirely by borrowing at £1.37m in 2025/26 and does not recur in the three-year forward plan. This is new borrowing for a demand-driven service.
findings.matters: Borrowing for temporary accommodation reflects current housing pressure; if demand continues, further borrowing may be needed, indicating ongoing budget stress in this area

findings.headline: Local Housing Company dominates capital programme with £21.062m spend in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Local Housing Company scheme represents £21.062m capital spending funded by borrowing/reserves in 2026/27, with £969k income, resulting in net £20.093m capital commitment. This single scheme accounts for 90% of the total net capital spending in that year.
findings.matters: A £20m capital investment signals material exposure to the performance of the housing company; a lender needs to understand the business case, expected revenue generation, and debt serviceability of this scheme

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation incomplete: three finance leases totalling £134k not yet reclassified to right-of-use assets
findings.detail: Auditors identified 10 finance leases (£1.75m net book value) that should have been reclassified to Right-of-Use assets under IFRS 16 at 1 April 2024. Seven were subsequently corrected following auditor discussion, but three assets totalling £134,367 in Land and Buildings and Community Infrastructure Assets remain to be reclassified, with management committing to action this in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Incomplete implementation of mandatory accounting standards indicates gaps in the council's control environment and financial reporting processes, with adjustments likely needed in the following year.
findings.figures: Three uncorrected lease assets £134,367; total identified leases £1.75m
findings.quote: We identified 10 finance leases classified under Land and Buildings (L&B) and community assets with a net book value of £1.75m that were not reclassified to Right-of-Use (RoU) assets on transition to IFRS 16. Following our discussion with management, 7 out of the 10 were reclassified. Three remaining assets of £134,367 under Land and buildings, Community and Infrastructure Assets are yet to be reclassified. Management confirmed these will be reclassified during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Prior year £2.085m accounting error from 2023/24 disclosed in 2024/25 comparatives without correction in original year
findings.detail: The 2023/24 audit identified a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was incorrectly recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS). This should have been expensed. Management chose not to adjust the 2023/24 financial statements at the time, resulting in that year's accounts being qualified. The error now appears as a comparator in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A significant accounting error that was known but not corrected demonstrates management was willing to accept material misstatement in the prior year, raising concerns about the rigour of the council's financial controls and accounting processes.
findings.figures: £2.085m prior period adjustment
findings.quote: The prior year error was a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS) and should have been expensed. Management had chosen not to adjust the 2023/24 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Audit opinion to be qualified due to material misstatement of prior year comparative arising from PPE disposal accounting
findings.detail: The auditor intends to issue an 'Except for' Qualification on the 2024/25 financial statements because a disposal of Property, Plant and Equipment was incorrectly processed during 2023/24 balances instead of being restated via opening balances. This is a material misstatement of the comparative figures. The same issue contributed to the 2023/24 accounts being qualified.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion signals control and financial reporting weaknesses, indicating the council's accounting systems may not reliably capture all transactions or may have gaps in the approval and classification process that creditors need to understand.
findings.figures: Material misstatement of comparative in 2024/25 financial statements
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be modified. We intend to issue an 'Except for' Qualification on the 2024/25 financial statements due to a material misstatement of the comparative arising from the accounting treatment of the disposal of an item of Property, Plant, and Equipment which should have been processed via a restatement of Opening Balances as opposed to it being transacted during the 2023/24 balances.

findings.paper_title: App IV - Swale_BC_Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: A 2023-24 improvement recommendation to map corporate risks to strategic objectives remains unaddressed after one year.
findings.detail: The auditor recommended in 2023-24 that the Council map risks identified in the Corporate Risk Register to the strategic objectives in the corporate plan. This recommendation was included to improve member visibility of which strategic priorities are most vulnerable to risk. As of March 2025, there is no evidence this has been implemented.
findings.matters: Unaddressed audit recommendations, especially when repeated, indicate either weak governance execution or capacity constraints. This pattern raises questions about the council's ability to implement management actions.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: A previous recommendation to map risks to strategic objectives remains outstanding, and we continue to advise its implementation to improve Member oversight. However, there is no evidence of this recommendation being addressed.

findings.paper_title: App IV - Swale_BC_Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: A prior-year accounting error of £2.085m from 2023-24 remains uncorrected, resulting in a modified audit opinion.
findings.detail: A £2.085m misclassification from 2023-24—where Kent County Council expenditure was incorrectly recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS)—was not corrected in the prior year accounts. The council chose not to adjust the 2023-24 financial statements. This error remains in the comparatives and results in a modified audit opinion on the 2024-25 statements.
findings.matters: An unrecorrected material error suggests governance gaps in financial reporting quality. A lender needs to understand whether this reflects process weakness or inability to correct identified issues.
findings.figures: £2.085m prior period adjustment
findings.quote: The prior year error was a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS) and should have been expensed. Management had chosen not to adjust the 2023-24 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: App IV - Swale_BC_Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Planning Services overspent by £0.9m in 2024-25, requiring offset from temporary savings and late grants.
findings.detail: Despite the council achieving an overall £0.317m surplus, Planning Services reported a £0.9m overspend. This was absorbed through temporary service-level savings and late-arriving housing grants rather than underlying demand management.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in a statutory service like planning suggest underlying demand or cost pressures that may recur. Using one-off grants to mask overspends is not a sustainable solution.
findings.figures: £0.9m overspend in Planning Services
findings.quote: A £0.9m overspend in Planning Services was offset by temporary savings and late housing grants.

findings.paper_title: App IV - Swale_BC_Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital programme experienced a £14.7m underspend in 2024-25, predominantly from Local Housing Company project delays.
findings.detail: The Council's £23.6m capital budget saw a £14.7m underspend, with £12.5m attributable to delays in the Local Housing Company housebuilding projects. The unspent capital has been re-profiled into 2025-26, suggesting either project management challenges or market/delivery constraints affecting the council's housing delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Capital slippage at this scale indicates the Council may face delivery challenges with major infrastructure and housing schemes. For lenders, this signals execution risk on council-led projects and delayed income benefits.
findings.figures: £23.6m capital budget; £14.7m underspend; £12.5m from Local Housing Company delays
findings.quote: The capital budget of £23.6m saw a £14.7m underspend due largely (£12.5m) to Local Housing Company housebuilding project delays. Spend has been re-profiled into 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: App IV - Swale_BC_Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The Council projects a £4.9m annual deficit by 2028-29 but has not adopted a formal long-term savings programme despite prior year recommendation.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy highlights a forecast annual deficit of £4.9m by 2028-29. The Council continues to identify savings within service budgets annually, but there remains no formal long-term savings programme. The auditor reiterated this as an improvement recommendation, noting that savings of this scale typically require transformational change with dedicated governance structures. For 2025-26, the Council is meeting a £0.677m deficit through reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a credible, structured plan to address its growing funding gap. Year-to-year budget patches without a multi-year savings strategy pose material sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £4.9m forecast annual deficit by 2028-29; £0.677m reserve drawdown in 2025-26 to balance budget
findings.quote: An annual forecast deficit of £4.9m by the end of the MTFS period to 2028-29 poses a challenge and, though strong planning and oversight support resilience, without a formal savings programme this will be a difficult challenge to meet.
